query_text: Should electroconvulsive therapy be used as a mental health treatment?

action.query: electroconvulsive therapy indications efficacy risks guidelines depression 2024 2025 APA NICE

annotations.title: Brain Stimulation Therapies - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)
Rapidly-Acting Treatments for Treatment-Resistant Depression (RAPID) - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

content.text:
**Yes—but only in specific circumstances, with careful consent and medical oversight.** Electroconvulsive therapy, or **ECT**, is a legitimate, evidence-based mental health treatment, not the same thing as the frightening “shock therapy” depictions from decades ago. Modern ECT is done under anesthesia, with muscle relaxants, monitoring, and controlled electrical stimulation.

ECT is most commonly considered for **severe major depression**, especially when depression is **life-threatening**, involves **psychosis**, severe refusal to eat/drink, catatonia, or **high suicide risk**, or when several medications/therapies have failed. It is also used in some cases of **bipolar disorder, mania, catatonia, and treatment-resistant psychiatric illness**. NIMH describes ECT as a brain stimulation treatment for serious mental disorders and notes it is sometimes used earlier when severe depression becomes life-threatening. ([nimh.nih.gov](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/brain-stimulation-therapies/brain-stimulation-therapies?utm_source=openai))

The main reason to use ECT is that it can work **quickly** and can be highly effective for severe or treatment-resistant depression. The American Psychiatric Association says ECT is most often used for severe major depression or bipolar disorder that has not responded to other treatments, and MedlinePlus describes it as highly effective for severe depression. ([psychiatry.org](https://www.psychiatry.org/patients-families/ect?utm_source=openai))

That said, ECT should **not** be treated casually or as a first-line option for mild or moderate symptoms. It has real burdens and risks: it requires anesthesia, repeated treatments, medical monitoring, and can cause short-term confusion, headache, nausea, muscle aches, and—most importantly—**memory problems**. Some people have temporary memory gaps; some report longer-lasting autobiographical memory loss. NIMH notes ECT works faster than many options but carries a risk of cognitive side effects and requires anesthesia and a surgical setting. ([nimh.nih.gov](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/research/research-funded-by-nimh/research-initiatives/rapidly-acting-treatments-for-treatment-resistant-depression-rapid?utm_source=openai))

So the balanced answer is:

- **Appropriate:** severe depression with suicidality, psychosis, catatonia, refusal to eat/drink, severe treatment-resistant depression, or urgent need for rapid response.
- **Usually not appropriate:** mild/moderate depression, anxiety alone, ordinary stress, or when less invasive treatments have not yet been tried unless there is a compelling emergency.
- **Essential safeguards:** informed consent when possible, discussion of alternatives, assessment of medical risks, cognitive/memory monitoring, use of the least risky effective technique, and a relapse-prevention plan afterward.

If this is about you or someone you know, the right next step is not deciding alone but getting an evaluation from a **psychiatrist experienced with ECT**, ideally with a second opinion if time allows. If there is immediate risk of suicide or inability to eat, drink, or stay safe, seek emergency help now—ECT can be one of the treatments considered in that kind of crisis.
